# leads

[arc reference](../index.md) › [Lanes](../index.md#lanes) › **Lane**

## Why it exists

```tagline
The careful salesperson. Twenty-five researched people instead of thousands, every message written for
one person, every send approved by a human. The machine is built; it has not yet met a real stranger.
```

# Start here

## In plain words

Think of arc as a small company whose staff are AI models. One thing every company eventually needs is
customers, and the lazy way to find them is to buy a huge list and send everyone the same email.

**The leads lane builds the opposite.** Picture one careful salesperson. They pick a small number of
people, find out why each one might need the product, and write each one a message that could only
have been written for them. Beside them stands a chaperone with a veto who never gets tired.

```panel big
**The chaperone is code, not a promise.** The daily limit, the "never contact this person again" list and the office-hours window are checked at the last second before every send, from the written record, not from a counter someone could edit. There is no switch to turn them off.
```

### What this lane is for

The lane's goal, from its plan (`initiatives/leads/PLAN.md`), is a command that turns a description of
the ideal customer into about twenty-five well-researched leads, not thousands. It drafts first
messages that cannot be a template blast. It then runs a capped sequence that a person approves send by
send. Every send, reply and block is written into arc's logbook, so it can be replayed later.

### The rule about private data

The people being researched are real, and this repo is public. So names, email addresses and drafts
live in a private store outside the repo folder (ADR-0410). The repo holds only the machinery. The
approver sees the drafted message, and the logbook never carries it (ADR-0412).

## arc words → normal words

```lede
Seven pieces of arc jargon. Each is an ordinary sales-desk thing wearing a technical name.
```

```rosetta
ICP | the description of the ideal customer | a file that the research step turns into a list of leads
dossier | one lead's file | why they fit, at least two source links, and a checked email address
provenance | where a fact was found | only an approved list of honest sources counts; a bought list does not
BELOW-BAR | "not dishonest, but thin" | a warning for a draft that is generic or too like another draft (ADR-0404)
suppression | the do-not-contact list | permanent, and triggered by an unsubscribe or a reply
L1 | a human approves every single send | the lowest trust level, and where the lane stays
rehearsal mode | a dress rehearsal with known friends | the real sending path, five owner-known addresses, marked so it never counts as a real campaign (ADR-0416)
```

## How one lead becomes one message

```lede
Each step can say no. A lead that fails early never reaches a draft, and a draft that fails never
reaches an inbox.
```

```flow
source: the customer description
box: ① Research | a dossier per lead
box: ② Draft | one message each
box: ③ Check | honest and specific?
box*: ④ Approve | a person says yes
labels: leads, drafts, passed
out: bad source | lead rejected, with the reason
out: unverified email | lead held, not guessed
out: generic draft | refused, or flagged
out+: -
divider: 3 | all inside arc | a real person is contacted
note: The send itself is the owner's keystroke. Caps and the do-not-contact list are checked once more at that moment.
caption: Figure 1 — from a description to a sent message. | The dashed line is where a stranger receives something.
```

## The stages, one by one

```lede
Each stage is written twice: first in ordinary words, then what actually happens.
```

```steps
t: Research a small list
plain: The research step finds people who fit, writes down why, and keeps the source links. A lead whose information came from a bought list or a login-walled page is turned away. An email that cannot be checked is held, never assumed good.
d: Provenance is a closed allowlist and unverifiable emails are HELD, not sent blind. The check is a live mail-server lookup plus syntax, not a paid vendor (ADR-0418).
f: `.claude/scripts/leads/arc-leads.mjs`

t: Write a message that is not a blast
plain: A message must mention something true and specific about that one person, and say why it matters to what is on offer. If it does not, it cannot even reach the approval queue. Thin or near-identical drafts get a warning instead.
d: The lint has a hard-fail class and a heuristic BELOW-BAR class, kept apart on purpose (ADR-0404).
f: `initiatives/leads/PLAN.md`

t: Keep the limits in code
plain: Twenty sends a day at most, two touches to one person per week, never after a reply, only in office hours. All of it is recounted from the written record at the moment of sending, so a hand-edited number changes nothing.
d: Caps and suppression derive from receipts and are re-checked at the send moment (ADR-0403). Sending is only ever to a dedicated domain (ADR-0402).
f: `initiatives/leads/PLAN.md`

t: Handle the replies
plain: A reply is read, sorted into a kind, and the sequence stops for that person before the next batch. An interested reply gets a draft calendar link in the same run. An unsubscribe blocks the person on the spot.
d: Replies are ingested from a file or standard input, never from the command line, and the plan ties each reply to a typed receipt.
f: `initiatives/leads/phases/phase-02-spec.md`
```

# The bigger loop

## A rehearsal, as a story

```loop
top: 1 | five known people
top: 5 | the logbook
stage: 1 · Owner names five | people he knows
stage: 2 · Research and draft | the real pipeline
stage: 3 · Gates run | facts, lint, allowlist
stage*: 4 · Owner approves | in the inbox
stage!: 5 · Send is attempted | the clock decides
labels: roster, dossiers, verdicts, yes
back: last -> 1 | a refusal is recorded too, so the next run starts from what really happened
caption: Figure 2 — the rehearsal, start to finish. | A refusal counts as the guard working.
```

1. The owner names five addresses he controls or knows.
2. The pipeline researches and drafts for each one.
3. The gates check the facts, the wording and the allowlist.
4. He approves each in the inbox.
5. The send is tried. If it is outside office hours, it is refused.

*This story is an illustration of the shape of a rehearsal. The tracker records a real one that reached step 5 and was refused for exactly that reason.*

## Where it stands

The tracker (`initiatives/leads/PROGRESS.md`) holds the live phase and burn in the generated sections.
In words: research, the sending guards, replies and arc's own notification mail are built and closed.
Each closed phase went through a hostile-input pass that found real holes, and the lane wrote them down.

The current phase is the rehearsal. A real run went from research to drafts to approval on five real
dossiers, and the owner approved all five. Every send was then refused by the office-hours window. That
is the guard working, not a fault. What is outstanding is one command, run by the owner inside office
hours from the main clone (the logbook refuses to be written from a worktree).

The real campaign is parked to a later cycle. It needs a named offer and about twenty-five real
recipients, and the owner could not yet supply either. Warming a sending domain with nothing to sell
was judged premature, so it was refused.

Two things in the tracker show the lane's habits. The appetite (its time budget) was extended in the
open when one phase overran, as a dated one-time decision. And the anti-template gate stopped its own
author: a hand-written batch of facts that were one template with a number changed was refused, and
the batch was replaced rather than the gate loosened.

What is next: the owner's send inside the window, then closing the rehearsal phase, and later the
real campaign.

## How it connects to the rest of arc

- **The logbook and the inbox.** Every send, reply and block is a receipt on the spine, and approvals
  go through `arc-inbox`, the same way every other lane does it.
- **arc's own mail.** The same sending transport is reused to email the owner about a failed deploy or a
  waiting approval, with its own policy and its own limits, kept apart from customer outreach (ADR-0415).
- **The public repo.** The private store exists so real people's details never become part of what a
  public repo could show (ADR-0410).

# Meta

## Glossary

```gloss
spine: arc's append-only logbook of what happened.
receipt: one typed entry on the spine, such as a send, a reply or a block.
journal: a crash-safe note of a send in flight, settled against the spine after a crash.
allowlist: a short list of the only addresses or sources that are allowed.
```
